title: Fairchild v. Hughes
lead: A citizen seeks to stop recognition and enforcement of the Nineteenth Amendment, but his general interest in lawful government supplies no personal right for an Article III case.

actors.name: Charles Fairchild
actors.role: New York citizen and taxpayer, also invoking membership in the American Constitutional League.

actors.name: The Secretary of State and Attorney General
actors.role: Federal officials whom Fairchild sought to restrain.

proceedings: The local trial court dismissed the bill on July 14, 1920; the D.C. Court of Appeals affirmed.
The Supreme Court affirmed on February 27, 1922, because the asserted interest did not present an Article III case.
limits: The Supreme Court did not decide the amendment’s ratification validity or adopt every part of the lower court’s proclamation rationale.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Fairchild tries to prevent recognition of the proposed amendment
sections.cue: What personal and public interests did he assert?
paragraphs: On July 7, 1920, Charles Fairchild sued the Secretary of State and Attorney General in the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia, then a local trial court. He claimed to represent citizens, taxpayers and members of the American Constitutional League, which advocated state control over voting qualifications.

He sought a declaration that the proposed Nineteenth Amendment was void and injunctions against its proclamation and enforcement, including interlocutory relief. His complaint alleged thirty-four legislative ratifications and another state’s certificate, challenged legislative ratification and particular states’ actions, and said the Secretary would proclaim adoption upon one more customary certificate because he lacked investigatory authority.

sections.title: Predicted election consequences form the basis of the complaint
sections.cue: Why did those allegations later prove insufficient?
paragraphs: Fairchild alleged that a proclamation would mislead state officials into admitting women to elections otherwise limited to men, dilute lawful votes and nearly double election expenses. He also attacked a proposed federal enforcement bill, anticipating prosecution of officials who excluded women. These were his allegations, not constitutional defects found by the Court.

The Attorney General’s predicted enforcement depended on legislation not yet enacted and would target election officials. Fairchild was not an election official. His own state, New York, already enfranchised women through its constitution and had ratified the federal amendment.

sections.title: The lower courts reject the suit as ratification proceeds
sections.cue: Which rationale did the appellate court use?
paragraphs: The trial court ordered the defendants to show cause concerning interlocutory relief. After their response and dismissal motion, it discharged that order and dismissed the bill on July 14, 1920. During Fairchild’s appeal, the Secretary received a thirty-sixth certificate and proclaimed adoption on August 26.

The D.C. Court of Appeals affirmed using its earlier Colby decision about the Eighteenth Amendment. That decision treated ratification as the source of constitutional validity and the proclamation as a required response to proper official notices. Fairchild then sought Supreme Court review.

sections.title: The Supreme Court affirms at the threshold
sections.cue: Why did it leave constitutional validity undecided?
paragraphs: Justice Brandeis’s opinion of February 27, 1922, found no need to examine the proclamation rationale. Putting a request in the form of an equity suit did not create an Article III case. Judicial power protected or enforced rights and prevented or redressed wrongs; Fairchild identified no personal right needing the requested intervention.

His remaining interest was the citizen’s general concern for lawful administration and avoidance of wasted public money. That did not authorize an individual to obtain a judicial ruling on an amendment or prospective statute indirectly through injunctions against officials. The Court affirmed the decree without deciding ratification validity or excluding a later suit by proper parties with an affected right. No separate opinion or participation qualification appeared.

sources.pinpoint: 129–130; Supreme Court reasoning and exact disposition
